list.listitem: All older persons should be asked about falls. Patients may not volunteer this information. B
Patients who have fallen or have a gait or balance problem are at higher risk of future falls. B
Screen for gait and balance in patients >65 years by observing them rise from a chair without using their arms, walk several paces, and return (the "Get Up and Go Test"). B
Exercise, vision assessment and treatment, Tai Chi, and environmental modification in the home can reduce the risk of future falls. A
Patients who have previously fallen may self-impose functional limitations due to fear of falling, which can lead to depression, helplessness, and social isolation. C

background.definition: A fall is any unintentional positional change that results in a patient coming to rest on the ground, floor, or other lower surface.

list.listitem: 30% to 40% of community dwelling, generally healthy people over the age of 65 fall annually.
Falls are the leading cause of fatal and nonfatal injuries among adults aged 65 years and older.
Incidence rates of falls for elderly living in nursing home and in hospitals are up to three times higher than for community dwelling elderly.
In 2019, the emergency department recorded 3 million visits for older adult falls

In 2015, the direct medical costs of falls for people 65 years and older in the United States was $637.2 million for fatal falls and $31.3 billion for non-fatal falls.In 2015, the average cost of a fatal fall was $26,340 while the average cost of a nonfatal fall was $9780.
In 2020, healthcare spending on non-fatal falls among community-dwelling older adults in the Uniited States was estimated at $80 billion,
Falls are the leading cause of nonfatal and unintentional injuries for older persons in the United States.
Up to 30% of falls cause serious injuries, such as head trauma or fractures.
Older adults are hospitalized for fall-related injuries five times more often than they are for injuries from other causes.
Recurrent falls and hip fractures are a common reason for the admission of previously independent elderly to long-term care facilities.

A systematic review revealed that between 59% and 78% of patients admitted to the hospital with vertebral fragility, the fracture was triggered by a preceeding fall or trauma. Older people and those with mulitple comorbidities were at higher risk of mortality and discharge to a care facility.
Falls in older adults appear to be a risk marker for subsequent motor vehicle collisions and related injury.
The cause of falls is often multifactorial.
Physiologic changes associated with aging, comorbidities that affect blood pressure and balance, medications, and environmental factors can all contribute.

A systematic review of 53 trials comparing a cholinesterase inhibitor (galantamine, rivastigmine, or donepezil) found that adults taking cholinesterase inhibitors were less likely to have falls than those taking placebo (5.3% vs 6.3%; NNT = 102; 95% CI 57 - 458), but they were more likely to have syncopal episodes (1.5% vs 0.8%; number needed to treat to harm = 142; 90 - 347). The rates of injuries and fractures were similar between groups.
See for a list of risk factors.
Ambulation depends on the complex integration of cognitive, neuromuscular, sensory, and skeletal components.
Physiologic changes associated with advancing age and/or disease may affect any or all of the components necessary for successful ambulation.
Environmental hazards contribute to the risk of falls.
Older persons (or their caregivers) should be asked at least once a year about falls by their health care professional. B

Older people who present for medical attention because of a fall, or report recurrent falls in the past year, or demonstrate abnormalities of gait and/or balance should be offered a multifactoral fall risk assessment. B

The USPSTF guideline on interventions to prevent falls (2024) concluded that exercise interventions provide a moderate net benefit (B recommendation) and that multifactorial interventions provide a small net benefit (C recommendation).

Data regarding the value of vitamin D supplementation is mixed. A Cochrane review concluded that vitamin D supplementation, exercise in subacute hospital settings, and multifactorial interventions in hospital settings can reduce the risk of falls. However, a more recent study randomized patients to 24,000 IU of vitamin D once monthly, 60,000 IU of vitamin D once monthly, or 24,000 IU vitamin D plus 300 mcg calcifediol. The high dose vitamin D group actually had a higher risk of falls than the other two groups.
In addition, the large VITAL randomized trial found no difference in the risk of fracture with vitamin D.

The USPSFT recommends against vitamin D supplementation to prevent falls in community dwelling adults 65 years old or older. These recommendations apply to community dwelling adults not known to have osteoporosis or vitmain D deficiency. B

A meta-analysis of exercise found that regular moderate intensity exercise 2 to 3 times per week decreases the overal likelihood of falls and resulting injuries in the elderly, but doesn't decrease the overall risk of hospitalization or of mortality.

A meta-analysis identified 19 studies with 3202 older particapants evaluating interventions to prevent falls. Exercise reduced the rate of falls (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.49-0.95) and the number of participants with 1 or more falls (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.98). However, the effect dissipated after the intervention period ended. There was also no significant reduction in fractures (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.24-2.20).
A meta-analysis of exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community found that exercise programs that reduce falls primarily involve balance and functional exercises.

An RCT of 456 patients found that home-based Tai Chi was more effective than lower extremity training/PT in preventing injurious falls (RR 0.41; 95% CI 0.20-0.83). Similarly, a systematic review of 10 studies with 2645 older participants at risk or with a history of falls found that Tai Chi decreased both the short-term (RR 0.57) and long-term (RR 0.87) risk of falls. A

A meta-analysis of fall prevention strategies in older adults identified 283 RCTs with 159,910 participants. They concluded that four interventions were associated with a significant reduction in injurious falls: exercise alone, exercise + vision assessment/treatment, exercise + vision assessment + environmental assessment/modification, and calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Of these, exercise and visual assessment/treatment was most effective. A
A meta-analysis of 6 RCTs and 3 other studies concluded that podiatric interventions can prevent falls (RR 0.73 to 0.77) but not injuries in community-dwelling elderly.
A meta-analysis concluded that at the organizational level, a combination of case management, patient reminder, and staff education can significantly reduce the likelihood of falls.

A systematic review of 49 studies found little evidence that medication review in community, long-term care facilities (LTCF), or hospital settings resulted in a lower fall risk. The strongest evidence was for medication reviews or deprescribing plans in LTCFs (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.72-1.02) for reducing number of persons having a fall.
Patients at risk of falling or who have fallen warrant a detailed fall-related assessment. B
The elements of an assessment include data about the circumstances of the falls(s), identification of risk factors for falls, medical comorbidities, functional status, and environmental risks. C
Patients with a history of two or more falls in the previous year, mobility impairment, reduced grip strength, and the presence of a depressive state are at risk for future falls. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Gait/balance problem, environmental hazard, visual impairment
Lightheadedness with change from sitting/supine to upright position
Abnormal gait, shuffling steps, orthostatic hypotension

list.listitem: A comprehensive fall evaluation should describe the circumstances surrounding recent falls, identify fall risk factors, delineate modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors, assess functional status, and target fall prevention strategies.
Ask about falls in the past year: frequency of falls, context, and characteristics of fall; eyewitness accounts; fear of falling.

A systematic review of 29 studies with 103,306 participants found that a patient report of "dizziness" is an independent predictor of any future falls (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.44-1.84) but no association with future injury falls (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.87-1.45).

The World Falls Algorithm identifies anyone with a fall in the last 12 months who has an injury, 2 or more falls in the past year, frailty, who is unable to get up from lying on the floor, and who had loss of conciousness or syncope as high risk for recurrent falls. Those patients should go through a more detailed risk assessment and may benefit from exercise and other interventions. Patients at intermediate risk had a fall, none of these risk factors, but a timed up and go of more than 15 seconds.
Review medications with particular attention to psychotropic medications and polypharmacy (greater than four medications may increase the risk of falls).

Ask about recent initiation of antihypertensive drugs and changes to theraoy. Multiple cohort studies have demonstrated a transient increased risk of fall at initiation of antihypertensive therapy or with dose increases.
Evaluate acute and chronic medical problems and screen for depression.
Physical examination should include vision screening; assessment of gait, balance, and mobility; and an assessment of cognition.
The neurological exam should include evaluation of lower extremity peripheral nerves; proprioception; reflexes; and cortical, extrapyramidal, and cerebellar function.
The cardiovascular exam should include heart rate and rhythm, postural pulse and blood pressure, and if indicated, blood pressure response to carotid sinus stimulation.

A systematic review found little evidence to support the use of simple instruments to evaluate patients for frailty. A normal gait speed and a normal timed up and go test had a good negative likelihood ratio (<0.1) for ruling out frailty.
The history, physical exam, and differential diagnosis regarding etiology of the fall(s) should guide utilization of further diagnostic testing.
A risk model, focusing attention on four intrinsic factors, predicts future falls for community dwelling elderly.
See .
A comprehensive fall evaluation should be performed on any older person who presents for medical attention because of a fall or reports recurrent falls in the past year.

For patients over 65 who have had a single fall or who have not already fallen, screening should consist of an assessment of gait and balance (gait and balance are the most studied risk factors for future falls and have more frequently predicted future falls than other domains).

Screen for gait and balance via the “Get Up and Go Test.” Persons are observed as they stand up from a chair without using their arms, walk several paces, and return. Those demonstrating no difficulty or unsteadiness need no further assessment.
Older people with recurrent falls or at increased risk of falling should be considered for individualized, multifactorial interventions to reduce the future risk of falls. A
Effective interventions include strength and balance training, home hazard assessment and intervention for patients with a history of falls, and combined exercise and vision assessment.. A
Medications should be reviewed and appropriately modified, with particular attention to psychotropic medications and polypharmacy (>4 medications). B
Patients who have fallen should have medications reviewed and altered or stopped as appropriate.

The STOPP/START program focuses on improving appropriate prescribing to elders. It was shown to result in fewer medications taken and lower cost, but did not reduce falls, hospitalizations, or functional status.
Polypharmacy (taking more than 4 medications daily) increases the risk for falls.
Withdrawal of psychotropic medications (neuroleptics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants) may reduce the incidence of falls.

In a meta-analysis of studies evaluating fall prevention strategies in community dwelling older adults, managing urinary incontinence increased the number of persons who fell (RR 1.39; 1.08 - 1.79), which is attritubute to the potential for hazardous medication use

A meta-analysis of 53 trials with 25,399 participants concluded that adults with neurocognitive disorders who take cholinesterase inhibitors are less likely to have falls (5.3% vs 6.3%, NNT = 100) but more likely to experience syncope (1.5% vs 0.8%, NNTH142) than adults who take placebo. There was no difference in fractures or injuries.
Pacemaker placement has demonstrated a small benefit in reducing syncope and falls in patients with carotid sinus syndrome.
Individualized muscle strengthening and balance re-training prescribed at home by a trained health professional is an important strategy to reduce future falls in adults.

A meta-analysis of exercise found that regular moderate intensity exercise 2 to 3 times per week decreases the overal likelihood of falls and resulting injuries in the elderly, but doesn't decrease the overall risk of hospitalization or of mortality.
Interventions that help improve balance may help reduced the risk of falls.
Tai Chi group exercises may be beneficial in reducing falls.
Yoga improves balance and flexibility, but its impact on falls in adults over the age of 60 is not known.
Supervised exercise programs reduce fall risk.

Home hazards assessment and modification by a professional, not alone but in conjunction with other interventions, may decrease falls. Use of carpet increases the risk of falls over vinyl flooring in a subacute ward.
Although the efficacy of treatment of remediable vision abnormalities for fall prevention is unknown, visual deficits should be addressed.

Most studies of these interventions have targetted persons with increased risk or previous falls. The largest study to date in an average risk population was an English cluster randomized trial with 9803 elderly patients. They found no reduction in falls or fractures with targeted exercise or multifarctorial intervention in addition to mailed information and screening for fall risk.

Following a stroke, there is moderately good evidence that vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) improves balance and gait for patients with balance or gait problems following stroke. On the basis of the available evidence, however, it is unclear whether VRT reduces the number of falls.
Behavioral and educational programs alone do not reduce falls.
They may nevertheless be of benefit if part of a multifactorial fall reduction intervention.
Complete evaluation of a patient’s fall risk and interventions to reduce falls may require referral to a clinician (i.e., a geriatrician) with skills and experience with fall assessment.
Hospitalization for hip fracture is associated with high morbidity and mortality.
Hip fracture in elderly patients is an important opportunity to reassess the patient's personal health-care priorities.
Institute measures to prevent delirium, venous thromboembolism, and prolonged use of indwelling bladder catheters in hospitalized patients.
Address osteoporosis and future fall prevention strategies.
Although the strategy is widely implemented, there are no adequate randomized control trials of multifactorial interventions to reduce falls among hospitalized inpatients.
There is no evidence that support the use of physical restraints (including bedrails) as a fall prevention strategy in older adults.
There is no evidence to support the universal use of hip protectors to prevent hip fractures among the elderly in health care centers.

Hip protectors may be used selectively, especially for patients with osteoporosis and risk factors for fall. A Cochrane review of 19 studies concluded that protectors have little or no effect on falls, and may decrease the risk of hip fractures while slightly increasing the risk of pelvic fractures. Compliance is an issue.
Interventions to promote the use of bed alarms to prevent falls in hospitalized patients increases the use of bed alarms but not the overall fall rates.
Despite a compelling rationale, evidence is scant that adding bedsode sitters to usual care reduces falls.

Among the recommendations of an interprofessional team of a program called Systems Addressing Frail Elder (SAFE) Care formed to address the risk factors associated with frailty among older adults newly admitted to a hospital, the most frequent included the implementation of a fall precautions protocol for 83.1% of patients.

A randomized control trial which included 390 participants 70 years old or greater demonstrated that tailored education provided in addition to usual care for patients admitted to hospital wards with a variety of diagnoses, including stroke, recent orthopedic surgery, general surgery, or general medical conditions did not significantly increase engagement of older adults in fall prevention strategies within 6 months after hospital discharge.

In a Cochrane systematic review of fall prevention strategies for older people in care facilities and hospitals, there was overall uncertainty of the effect of multiple strategies on the rate of falls and/or reducing the risk of falling. These strategies included exercise, general medication review, multifactorial interventions; physiotherapy, and providing bed sensor alarms.
Patients who have fallen once are at increased risk of falling again. A
Each fall has a risk of serious injury. C
Patients who have previously fallen may self-impose functional limitations due to fear of falling, which can lead to depression, helplessness, and social isolation. C
Engaging older adults is essential for prevention of falls and injuries: understanding their beliefs, attitudes and priorities about falls and their management is crucial to successfully intervening.
Falling happens more as people get older.
Falls are the leading cause of injury in adults 65 year old or older.
Patients who have fallen or have a fear of falling should tell their health care provider.
There are interventions that can prevent patients from falling.
